title: Response of a comprehensive climate model to a broad range of external forcings: relevance for deep ocean ventilation and the development of late Cenozoic ice ages
problem: Prior climate modeling experiments on ice age ocean circulation are heterogeneous and often inconsistent, making it difficult to gain a comprehensive appreciation for the relative importance and interactions of external forcings like CO2, orbital changes, and ice sheet size on the deep ocean.
method: This study uses a comprehensive Earth system model, integrated to equilibrium under a matrix of 40 combinations of CO2, orbital, and ice sheet forcings, to map out the large-scale behavior of deep ocean circulation and its role in late Cenozoic ice ages.
task: The task is to investigate the response of deep ocean circulation to a broad range of external forcings (CO₂, orbital parameters, ice sheet size) using an Earth system model to understand the development of late Cenozoic ice ages.

innovation: This paper provides a comprehensive view of how CO₂, orbital forcing, and ice sheet size influence deep ocean ventilation by integrating an Earth system model to equilibrium under 40 different combinations of these external forcings relevant to late Cenozoic ice ages.

kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: The model we use is CM2Mc, a coarser-resolution configuration of the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's ESM2M model (Dunne et al. 2012), which captures critical aspects of the Southern Ocean circulation (Russell et al. 2006).

The simulations use the coupled ocean-atmosphere-ice-biogeochemistry model CM2Mc.v2. In brief, this includes: a finite volume atmospheric model, similar to that used in the GFDL ESM2 models (Dunne et al. 2012); MOM5, a non-Boussinesq ocean model with a fully-nonlinear equation of state, parameterizations for mesoscale (Griffies 1998) and submesoscale (Fox-Kemper et al. 2008) turbulence, and parameterizations for vertical mixing due to boundary layer turbulence (Large et al. 1994) and to the breaking of internal tides above rough topography (Simmons et al. 2004); a sea-ice module; a static land module; and a coupler to exchange fluxes between the components.
